comments.text: Canadian here. I live in a part of a province in which there are literally no homes, detached or townhomes, for sale under 1 million. My parents bought their first home in 1973 for $40,000. That same home was listed a few years ago for 1.4 million dollars. It backs on to a railroad track. Their second home they bought in 1981 for $140, 000.00 is now valued at 1.7 million dollars. It sits beside a field of hydro towers and two major highways. That’s insanity. A great deal of this is due to disastrous government policies that allowed foreign investors to buy up an insane number of residential properties and turn them into rental properties. Also, it comes down to this: it isn’t the house that drives the prices here; it’s the land/lot that the house sits on that drives the price. It is common to see old tiny run down homes here priced at $1 million because it’s the lot (which is often not outstanding) that drives the price. People buy the lot for 1million, tear it down, build a monstrosity on it, and then price it at 3 million dollars. A 3 million dollar monstrosity surrounded by tiny old homes priced at 1 million dollars. My father used to say, “Invest in land because they’re not making any more of it.” It’s also disturbing how many people turned the idea of a home into another money making scheme.

comments.text:
Unfortunately this phenomenon of regular people seeing housing as a business has spread to El Salvador. It's even worse because housing prices have skyrocketed because people here buy overpriced tiny apartments to either turning them into Airbnbs or to sell them to Americans who probably can't afford homes in their country. Thing is, the prices are not too far away from what you guys have now. We are being gentrified by foreigners in our own country and rich people just see the dollar signs. But it's a bubble. We're a tiny country with only one large city where most of the office jobs are. What are you going to do once all young professionals live too far away from your office for it to be feasible for them to commute?

It's a domino effect, because a lot of professionals I know, myself included, are so burnt out with everything were just going independent and selling our services internationally. I'm very experienced in my field, but I feel for the younger generation and the challenges they have ahead. Hopefully this stupid bubble will pop and people will be able to afford housing again.
